slides.headline: Desk posture: what Pilates really trains
slides.sub: Not one perfect position. More ways to move comfortably.

slides.title: No single right posture
slides.body: Current evidence suggests no one sitting position protects your back or neck. Comfort usually comes from changing positions often and having the strength to sit for longer.

slides.title: Upper back strength
slides.body: Reformer rows, arm work and swan prep train the muscles between your shoulder blades, which can make long stretches at the screen feel less draining.

slides.title: Mobility for a rounded day
slides.body: Spine twists, mermaid stretches and chest openers move you in the directions desk work doesn't. Many people feel noticeably looser after even a short session on the reformer.

slides.title: Body awareness at work
slides.body: Pilates teaches you to notice when you've slumped, clenched or held your breath. That awareness makes it easier to reset during the day without forcing yourself upright.

slides.title: A two-minute desk reset
slides.body: Sit tall, take three slow breaths, then do five seated twists each way and five shoulder blade squeezes. Try it at the end of every meeting this week.

slides.headline: Desk days feeling heavy?
slides.body: Our Pilates team builds programs around desk life, starting with an assessment. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Pilates won't give you one perfect desk posture, and that's a good thing.

Current evidence suggests no single sitting position protects your back or neck. What tends to help is changing position often and having the strength and mobility to sit comfortably for longer.

Clinical Pilates builds upper back strength, moves your spine in the directions desk work skips, and helps you notice when you've slumped or started holding your breath. Try a two-minute reset after each meeting: three slow breaths, five seated twists each way and five shoulder blade squeezes.
